title: Hydraulic Cylinder Force
description: Explore how cap-end pressure and circular piston diameter determine ideal theoretical extension force in an internal visual pilot.

firstScreen.purpose: Change pressure or piston diameter and see the ideal theoretical extension force respond.

inputs.label: Pressure
inputs.validation: Reject non-finite values and constrain values to the reviewed educational interaction range.
inputs.educationalDescription: Controls the uniform cap-end pressure used by the ideal force model.

inputs.label: Piston diameter
inputs.validation: Reject non-finite values and constrain values to the reviewed educational interaction range.
inputs.educationalDescription: Controls the circular cap-end piston area used by the ideal force model.

outputs.label: Cap-end pressure
outputs.interpretation: The applied uniform pressure state at the cylinder cap end.

outputs.label: Cap-end piston area
outputs.interpretation: The circular area calculated from the current piston diameter.

outputs.label: Theoretical extension force
outputs.interpretation: The ideal theoretical cap-end extension force, not a rated available force.
outputs.warning: The model excludes losses, dynamics, component ratings and machine geometry.

learningOutcomes: Explain how cap-end pressure acting over piston area produces ideal theoretical extension force.
Use piston diameter to calculate circular cap-end area in SI units.
Predict how pressure and piston diameter affect theoretical force.
Configure an idealised pressure-and-diameter state that meets a stated opposing-force target.
State why this ideal relationship is not a complete cylinder or machine design model.

blocks.text: This internal pilot models ideal theoretical cap-end extension force and remains Engineering review required.
Allow about 20 minutes for interaction and 10 minutes for the check and optional deeper explanation.
Foundational: introductory fluid pressure, circular area and explicit SI conversion.
Complete the basic fluid-pressure lesson before this visual pilot.
Connect pressure and cap-end piston area to ideal theoretical extension force, calculate the circular area from diameter, and state the model limitations.
Hydraulic cylinders convert fluid pressure into mechanical force, but real actuator and machine performance requires more than the ideal pressure-area relationship.

blocks.definition: For this extension-only pilot, the full circular piston face exposed to cap-end pressure.

blocks.text: The visual binds one normal-state pressure, circular cap-end area and ideal theoretical force result across the gauge, cutaway, vector, schematic and text summary.
Pressure alone does not define cylinder force; the effective pressurised area is also required. Detailed assumptions and exclusions are retained in Deep Dive.

blocks.title: Training model only
blocks.text: This lesson does not establish equipment ratings, inspection procedures, operating permission or professional design sufficiency. Pressurised hydraulic equipment requires authorised procedures and supervision.
Complete the six concise questions after the visual experience. The separate formal assessment remains authenticated and server scored.
For the ideal cap-end extension case, pressure acts over the full circular piston area to produce theoretical force. Real available force and machine capacity require additional reviewed models.

blocks.text: Continue to flow and cylinder-speed fundamentals only after a reviewed kinematic model is available.

blocks.explanation: A larger circular piston diameter produces a larger cap-end area, so the ideal theoretical force increases at the same pressure.

blocks.hint: Look at the squared diameter term in the area equation.
blocks.explanation: Circular area depends on diameter squared, and that area then multiplies pressure in the ideal force equation.

blocks.title: Pressure, area and force
blocks.description: A concise sourced explanation of the ideal extension relationship.
blocks.principle: Cap-end pressure acts over the full circular piston area. A larger pressure or area produces a larger ideal theoretical extension force; pressure alone is not enough to determine force.
blocks.expandedExplanation: Starting from pressure as force per area, rearranging gives force as pressure multiplied by area. This lesson derives the circular cap-end area from piston diameter, converts all inputs explicitly to SI units, and excludes rod-side area and real losses.
blocks.safetyInformation: The result is not an equipment rating, certified lifting capacity or operating instruction.

blocks.title: Excavator boom cylinder
blocks.description: An original simplified visual connects the pressure-area concept to an excavator boom cylinder without importing product dimensions or ratings.
blocks.principle: The hydraulic system supplies pressurised fluid to a boom cylinder. Pressure acting on the piston contributes linear force that moves the boom through its mounting and linkage; the ideal pressure-area result alone does not predict lifting capacity.

accessibility.label: Simplified excavator boom and hydraulic cylinder
accessibility.textAlternative: A side-view line drawing identifies a hydraulic cylinder between an excavator body and boom. It does not show real dimensions or capacity.

accessibility.reducedMotionFallback: The application is a static SVG.

blocks.prompt: At fixed piston area, what happens to ideal theoretical extension force when pressure doubles?
blocks.answerExplanation: For F = p × A with area fixed, force changes in direct proportion to pressure.

blocks.prompt: Which quantity must be known with pressure to calculate ideal cylinder force?
blocks.answerExplanation: The ideal relationship requires pressure and effective pressurised area.

blocks.prompt: Which pair uses the internal SI units required by the force calculation?

options.text: Pressure in Pa and area in m².
Pressure in MPa and diameter in mm without conversion.
Force in kW and area in litres.

blocks.answerExplanation: The engineering calculation receives pressure in pascals and area in square metres after explicit conversion.

blocks.prompt: At fixed pressure, which visual reading changes when piston diameter increases?

options.text: Piston area and theoretical force both increase.
The source becomes a flow meter.

blocks.answerExplanation: Diameter changes circular area, and at fixed pressure that changes the ideal theoretical force.

blocks.prompt: What ideal theoretical force results from 5,000,000 Pa acting on 0.002 m²?
Why does the ideal cylinder-force result not establish an excavator's boom lifting capacity?

options.text: Machine performance also depends on linkage geometry, load position, losses, mounting and system conditions.
Hydraulic cylinders never act on excavator booms.
Pressure and area have no relationship to force.

blocks.answerExplanation: The ideal pressure-area result describes cylinder force only. A machine-level capacity calculation needs additional reviewed geometry, load, loss and structural models.

blocks.title: Derivation, units and model limits
blocks.description: Optional detail preserves the derivation, SI reasoning and excluded real-world effects.
blocks.content: Pressure is force per area, so rearranging p = F/A gives F = pA. For a circular cap-end piston, A = πD²/4. Pa × m² reduces to N because Pa is N/m². This pilot excludes rod-side annular area, friction, leakage, acceleration, buckling, mounting geometry, component ratings and machine lifting capacity.

accessibility.label: Optional hydraulic force derivation and limitations
accessibility.textAlternative: Expandable text derives the ideal relationship and lists excluded effects.

blocks.text: Pressure is treated as uniform over the circular cap-end piston area, with explicit SI inputs and no rod-side or loss model.
An ideal theoretical cylinder-force result is an educational relationship, not a certified available force, cylinder selection or machine capacity.
